question_papers.paper_title: Set 1 - Earth, Moon, and the Sun (NCERT Standard Practice Set)

questions.question_text: A Solar Eclipse occurs only on a:
Which term is defined as: 'Sun --- Moon --- Earth (Moon obstructs solar light).'?

sections.section_name: Section B (Short Answer Questions - 3 Marks Each)

questions.question_text: Why do we always see the same side/face of the Moon from Earth?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: The Moon's rotation period on its own axis exactly equals its orbital revolution period around Earth (~27.3 days), a phenomenon known as tidal locking or synchronous rotation.

questions.question_text: Describe the practical activity with aim: 'To model solar and lunar eclipse shadow geometries using a torch and spheres.'. Outline key steps and conclusion.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Steps: Align torch light, small ball, and large globe in a straight line in a dark room., Observe shadow of small ball falling on large globe (Solar Eclipse simulation)., Re-position large globe between torch and small ball to observe globe shadow covering small ball (Lunar Eclipse simulation).
Conclusion: Eclipses are natural shadow formations resulting from linear alignment of Sun, Earth, and Moon.

sections.section_name: Section C (Long Answer & Case Study - 5 Marks Each)

questions.question_text: Explain how Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt and revolution around the Sun cause summer and winter seasons in Northern and Southern hemispheres.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane. 2. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun (June Solstice), it receives direct solar rays for longer hours, causing Summer in the North and Winter in the South. 3. Six months later (December Solstice), Northern Hemisphere tilts away from Sun receiving indirect slanted rays, causing Winter in the North and Summer in the South.

questions.question_text:
Case Scenario: An astronomer in Delhi observes a Total Solar Eclipse lasting 3 minutes, while an astronomer in Chennai sees only a Partial Solar Eclipse at the same time.
Question: Why did Delhi experience totality while Chennai experienced only a partial eclipse?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Delhi was located within the narrow central umbral shadow cone cast by the Moon, blocking 100% of the Sun. Chennai was located in the broader penumbral shadow zone, where only part of the Sun was obstructed.

C) Completely independent of environmental variables
questions.correct_answer: A) Governed by precise natural physical/chemical laws

questions.question_text: Which concept corresponds to: 'Sun --- Earth --- Moon (Earth obstructs light reaching Moon).'?

sections.section_name: Section B (Short Answer Questions - 3 Marks Each)

questions.question_text: Why do solar and lunar eclipses NOT occur every single New Moon and Full Moon day?
questions.marking_scheme_answer: The Moon's orbital plane around Earth is tilted at an angle of ~5 degrees relative to Earth's orbital plane around the Sun. Most New and Full Moons pass slightly above or below the Sun-Earth line, avoiding eclipse alignment.

questions.marking_scheme_answer: Just as a passenger on a clockwise merry-go-round sees surrounding trees spinning anti-clockwise, an observer on Earth rotating from West to East sees celestial bodies (Sun, stars) moving in the opposite direction from East to West.

questions.marking_scheme_answer: Correct Fact: Seasons are caused by Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt during revolution, changing angle and duration of sunlight, NOT by distance variation from the Sun.

questions.question_text: Outline the procedure and observations for investigating Earth, Moon, and the Sun in the laboratory.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Procedure: Align torch light, small ball, and large globe in a straight line in a dark room., Observe shadow of small ball falling on large globe (Solar Eclipse simulation)., Re-position large globe between torch and small ball to observe globe shadow covering small ball (Lunar Eclipse simulation).
Observations: In position 1, small ball blocks light, casting a shadow on globe. In position 2, large globe blocks light, submerging small ball in darkness.
